opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's an interesting question, because if you look back at OpenAI in its early days, around 2016 and 2017, agents were really the center of everything. The mainstream belief then was that the path to general intelligence would run through reinforcement learning: you build an agent, put it in an environment, let it interact and get rewards, and intelligence emerges from that loop. That's why you saw OpenAI Gym, Universe, the Dota 2 project, robotic hand manipulation, and the multi-agent work like hide-and-seek that I was involved in. The intuition was that an agent acting in the world was the core object of study.

What happened later is that the field found a different entry point. GPT showed that you could first get a huge amount of general knowledge and reasoning ability from pretraining on internet text, without designing environments and rewards from scratch. In hindsight, the early RL agents were trying to learn everything from zero, so they were extremely sample-inefficient and very narrow. A Dota agent could beat world champions but couldn't do anything else.

So when OpenAI later described its five levels, chatbots, then reasoners, then agents, then innovators, then organizations, I see it as the original agent vision coming back, but in a different order. You first need a strong foundation model that understands language and the world, which is level one. Then you need it to reason and think over longer horizons, which is what the o-series models brought by applying RL on top of language models. Only then does the agent level really become feasible, because now the model has enough common sense and reasoning to act in open-ended environments like browsers, codebases, or operating systems.

In a sense, the early ambition wasn't wrong; it was premature. The goal of autonomous agents that can complete complex tasks was always there. What was missing was the prior knowledge. Reinforcement learning didn't go away either. It came back as the key technique for turning a pretrained model into a reasoner and then into an agent. So I'd say the five-level framework is almost a reconciliation of OpenAI's two eras: the GPT era supplied the foundation, and the RL and agent era supplies the ability to act.

And the later levels, innovators and organizations, connect directly to the multi-agent ideas from back then. Once you have capable individual agents, the natural next question is how many agents collaborate, compete, and divide labor, which is what we were exploring in simple environments years ago. Now it may become a practical question rather than a toy one.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the early agent vision with the later five-level framework, but does not say the early ambitions were less clearly defined or that the later classification was clearer.

r002.rationale: It says early OpenAI believed general intelligence could emerge through reinforcement-learning agents interacting with environments and receiving rewards.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think "agent" was actually baked into OpenAI's DNA from almost the very beginning, long before it became a buzzword. When I was there, around 2017 to 2018, the whole organization was essentially a reinforcement learning lab. The flagship projects were things like OpenAI Five for Dota 2 and the robotic hand solving a Rubik's cube. Those are agents in the most literal sense: a system that perceives an environment, takes actions, gets feedback, and improves over a long horizon. The language model work was a comparatively small group at the time. So the original ambition was never just "build a model that predicts the next token." It was "build something that can act in the world and achieve goals."

What changed was the path, not the destination. The bet that paid off was that scaling language models gave you a general prior about the world, a kind of universal foundation, much faster than training agents from scratch in individual environments. GPT came first because it was the more scalable road, but the people who built it still had the agent vision in the back of their minds.

So when the five-level framework came out, with chatbots at level one, reasoners at two, agents at three, innovators at four, and organizations at five, I read it less as a new strategy and more as the company making its original roadmap explicit. Level one and two are about the model being able to talk and then think. Level three is where you close the loop from the old RL days: the model has to take actions, observe consequences, and sustain a task over hours or days rather than a single turn. That is exactly the problem Dota and the robotic hand were about, just now with a language model as the brain instead of a narrow policy network.

The honest subtlety is that agents in the RL era and agents in the LLM era share the same definition but face different bottlenecks. Back then the hard part was exploration and sample efficiency in one environment. Now the hard part is reliability, long-horizon memory, and tool use across many open-ended environments. Levels four and five are what happens if you solve that: an agent that can do research on its own, and eventually a system that coordinates many agents like a company would. So I see the classification as a continuation. The early ambition was agents, the detour was language, and the five levels are the attempt to connect those two threads back together.

r001.rationale: The response calls the five-level framework a way to make the original roadmap explicit, but does not distinguish less clearly defined early ambitions from the later classification’s clarity.

r002.rationale: It describes OpenAI as essentially a reinforcement learning lab whose early projects pursued agents that act in the world and achieve goals, conveying aspirations for what RL could accomplish.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish the ambition from the milestone. OpenAI’s early interest in agents was about moving beyond a system that answers questions toward one that can take actions and carry out tasks. In the later five-level framework, agents occupy the third level, after chatbots and reasoners, with innovators and organizations beyond them.

From that perspective, agents were an important intermediate goal: intelligence becoming useful through action. But I wouldn’t assume that the later framework was already fully formed at the beginning. It gives us a way to interpret that early ambition, rather than proof that there was always a fixed roadmap.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the early ambition to build agents with the later five-level framework, saying the framework was not fully formed at the beginning and is a later way to interpret that ambition.

r002.rationale: The response describes early agents as systems that take actions and carry out tasks, but does not connect that pursuit to what reinforcement learning could achieve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the five-level framework helps clarify what OpenAI was aiming for early on. In that framework, you move from chatbots to reasoners, then agents, then innovators, and finally systems that can do the work of an organization. So an agent is already a step beyond a system that simply answers questions: it can take a goal, interact with an environment, and carry out a sequence of actions.

Looking back, I would interpret the early ambition in that broader sense. The goal wasn’t just to make conversation more fluent; it was to build systems that could actually get things done. But I wouldn’t assume the five-level roadmap was explicitly laid out from the beginning. It’s a later way of describing that trajectory, and it makes clear that agents are an important milestone rather than the endpoint.

r001.rationale: The response says the five-level roadmap was not necessarily explicit from the beginning and describes it as a later framework that clarifies the trajectory.

r002.rationale: It describes early agent ambitions as building systems that get things done, but does not connect those ambitions to what reinforcement learning could achieve.
